title: Can Kafka and Solace be used together — yes, many companies use Kafka as the durable system of record for long-term event retention and replay, and Solace for dynamic event distribution and selective routing to consumers — they solve different problems and are often complementary?
shortTitle: Can Kafka and Solace be used together, and why are they often complementary?

s1_definition.profdef: Yes, Kafka and Solace are frequently used together because they solve different problems and complement each other. Kafka serves as the durable system of record: a partitioned, append-only log that retains events for the long term and supports deterministic replay, event sourcing, and stream processing. Solace serves as the dynamic distribution layer: a broker-native hierarchical router that delivers precisely filtered slices to many heterogeneous consumers with low latency and without creating new topics. A common pattern bridges them, so an event flows through Solace for real-time selective routing while also landing in Kafka for durable retention and later replay.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India using two services together. Solace is the smart mail room that instantly sorts each incoming letter to exactly the desks that asked for that kind of letter, as desks keep changing their requests. Kafka is the permanent records vault where a copy of every letter is filed in order and kept for years, so auditors can replay the entire history whenever they need. The mail room makes sure the right person gets the right letter now; the vault makes sure nothing is ever lost and everything can be reconstructed later. You want both: fast, flexible delivery today and a durable, replayable record forever.
s1_definition.oneliner: Solace routes live events flexibly to the right consumers now; Kafka durably stores every event for replay later, and bridging them gives you both.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Yes, Kafka and Solace are frequently used together because they solve different problems and complement each other. Kafka serves as the durable system of record: a partitioned, append-only log that retains events for the long term and supports deterministic replay, event sourcing, and stream processing. Solace serves as the dynamic distribution layer: a broker-native hierarchical router that delivers precisely filtered slices to many heterogeneous consumers with low latency and without creating new topics. A common pattern bridges them, so an event flows through Solace for real-time selective routing while also landing in Kafka for durable retention and later replay.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India using two services together. Solace is the smart mail room that instantly sorts each incoming letter to exactly the desks that asked for that kind of letter, as desks keep changing their requests. Kafka is the permanent records vault where a copy of every letter is filed in order and kept for years, so auditors can replay the entire history whenever they need. The mail room makes sure the right person gets the right letter now; the vault makes sure nothing is ever lost and everything can be reconstructed later. You want both: fast, flexible delivery today and a durable, replayable record forever.

**One line to remember:** Solace routes live events flexibly to the right consumers now; Kafka durably stores every event for replay later, and bridging them gives you both.

sections.s2_technical:
The reason they combine well is that their design centres are different. Kafka optimises for a durable, ordered, partitioned log with long retention, offset-based replay, per-key ordering, and a stream-processing ecosystem. Solace optimises for broker-side hierarchical routing with wildcard subscriptions, low-latency fan-out, multi-protocol access, and dynamic filtering without topic creation. When a system needs both durable history and flexible live routing, using each for its strength is cleaner than forcing one to do both.

There are a few concrete integration patterns. The first is a bridge or connector that moves events between the two. Solace provides bridging capabilities, and Kafka has Kafka Connect, so you can run a connector that consumes from Solace and produces to Kafka, giving every routed event a durable home, or the reverse, publishing Kafka events into Solace for selective fan-out. For example, a transaction event can be published once, selectively delivered to desks via Solace wildcard subscriptions, and simultaneously captured into a Kafka `transactions` topic for seven-year retention.

The second pattern is Solace-in-front, Kafka-behind. The producer publishes to Solace, where the broker routes slices to live consumers such as trading desks, and a sink bridge persists the full stream into Kafka. Live consumers get only their slice with low latency; Kafka holds the complete ordered record for compliance and analytics. This avoids topic proliferation on the Kafka side because the fine routing happens in Solace, and it avoids consumer-side waste because desks do not each read everything.

The third pattern is Kafka-as-source, Solace-as-distribution. Events are produced into Kafka as the system of record, and a bridge republishes selected streams into Solace for dynamic, content-shaped distribution to many consumers whose interests change. Here Kafka guarantees durability and replay while Solace handles the flexible last-mile delivery.

The senior nuances matter in a bank. First, think about ordering and delivery guarantees across the bridge: Kafka gives per-partition ordering keyed by, say, account id, and you must decide how that maps to Solace delivery and whether the bridge preserves ordering and handles duplicates idempotently. Second, think about the system of record principle: pick one source of truth, usually Kafka, so that if the two diverge you know which one is authoritative and can replay Kafka to rebuild. Third, think about back-pressure and retention mismatches: Solace may drop or age out messages faster than Kafka retains them, so the durable copy must be the long-horizon one. Fourth, monitor the bridge itself as a first-class component, because a stalled bridge silently breaks either durability or live delivery.

So the answer is a clear yes, and the reason is that they are complementary rather than competing. Solace handles dynamic event distribution and selective routing to changing consumers; Kafka handles durable long-term retention, replay, event sourcing, and stream processing. Many enterprises run exactly this split, often with a bridge connecting them, choosing one as the authoritative system of record.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India publishes a firm-wide transaction event stream and needs two outcomes at once.

Problem 1 — Many trading and operations desks each want a different, often-changing slice of the live transaction feed delivered immediately, such as all Mumbai transactions or all large transactions, and they must not trigger a new topic every time their interest changes. This is exactly Solace's job: publish into a hierarchical namespace and let each desk's wildcard subscription receive its slice with low latency.

Problem 2 — Compliance requires that every transaction event be stored durably for seven years and be replayable so the full ledger can be rebuilt at any time. This is exactly Kafka's job: append every event to a retained, ordered log that supports offset-based replay.

Problem 3 — The bank does not want to publish twice or maintain two divergent truths. It wants one publish that both routes live and persists durably, with Kafka as the single authoritative system of record. This is exactly the bridge pattern: an event enters Solace for routing and a sink bridge captures the same stream into Kafka.

The demo models this complementary architecture. A `SolaceRouter` publishes events into a hierarchical namespace and delivers matching slices to subscribed desks. A `SolaceToKafkaBridge` observes every event Solace receives and persists it into a `KafkaSystemOfRecord`, which retains events in an append-only log and supports replay from the beginning. The `main` method publishes several transactions, shows desks receiving only their slices live, shows the bridge persisting every event, and then shows compliance replaying the full ordered history from Kafka to rebuild the ledger.

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  application:
    name: event-backbone-service
solace:
  msgVpn: txn-vpn            # dynamic routing, no topic creation
kafka:
  bootstrap-servers: kafka-1:9092
  system-of-record-topic: transactions
  retention: 7y             # authoritative durable store
bridge:
  source: solace
  sink: kafka
  preserve-order: true      # key by accountId across the bridge
```

##### 4f. Logging notes

Live Solace deliveries and Kafka appends are logged at `info` so you can see both the flexible routing and the durable capture happening from a single publish; the bridge's internal capture step is logged at `fine`. Replay is logged at `info` with offsets to show deterministic reconstruction.
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two desk subscriptions (Mumbai operations on everything under Mumbai, and a large-transaction monitor on any large transaction) and four transaction events, keyed by account id for ordering.

Step 1: Both desks register their subscription patterns in Solace. Kafka's transactions topic is empty. The bridge is wired so that every event Solace receives will be captured into Kafka.

Step 2: The first event, a small Mumbai debit for Rajesh, is published once. Solace tests the patterns: Mumbai operations matches on the Mumbai branch, so it is delivered live to that desk; the large monitor does not match because the band is small. The same event is then handed to the bridge, which appends it to Kafka at offset zero.

Step 3: The second event, a large Mumbai transfer for Rajesh, is published. Mumbai operations matches on branch and the large monitor matches on band, so both desks receive it live. The bridge appends it to Kafka at offset one, keyed by Rajesh's account so his events stay ordered.

Step 4: The third event, a large Sao Paulo credit for Priya, is published. Mumbai operations does not match because the branch is not Mumbai, but the large monitor matches on band, so only the monitor receives it live. The bridge appends it to Kafka at offset two.

Step 5: The fourth event, a small London fee for Priya, matches neither desk, so no live delivery happens, but the bridge still appends it to Kafka at offset three. This is the crucial point: Solace filtered it out for live delivery, yet the durable record kept it anyway.

Step 6: Later, compliance replays Kafka from the start. All four events are re-read in offset order, regardless of which desks saw them live, allowing the full ledger to be rebuilt deterministically. Solace gave the right slice to the right desk in real time; Kafka kept the complete, replayable truth.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, Kafka and Solace are very commonly used together, and the reason is that they solve different problems and complement each other rather than compete. Kafka is the durable system of record: a partitioned, append-only log that retains events for the long term and supports deterministic offset-based replay, event sourcing, and a stream-processing ecosystem. Solace is the dynamic distribution layer: a broker-native hierarchical router that delivers precisely filtered slices to many heterogeneous consumers with low latency and without anyone creating new topics as consumer interests change.

The way they fit together is usually a bridge. A single transaction event is published once, Solace routes it live to exactly the desks whose wildcard subscriptions match, and a sink bridge, often built with Kafka Connect or Solace's own bridging, captures the same stream into a Kafka topic that is retained for years. Live consumers get only their slice with low latency and without topic proliferation, while Kafka keeps the complete, ordered, replayable record for compliance, analytics, and ledger reconstruction. A key design point is that even events that matched no live subscription are still persisted to Kafka, so the durable record is complete regardless of who was listening at the time.

The senior nuances I always raise are, first, choose one authoritative system of record, normally Kafka, so that if the two ever diverge you know which is the source of truth and can replay Kafka to rebuild. Second, decide how ordering maps across the bridge, keying Kafka by something like account id so per-account order is preserved, and make the bridge idempotent against duplicates. Third, watch for retention mismatches, since Solace may age messages out faster than Kafka retains them, which is precisely why the durable copy belongs in Kafka. And fourth, monitor the bridge as a first-class component, because a stalled bridge silently breaks either durability or live delivery.

At National Bank of India this was the exact architecture we used. Trading and operations desks wanted diverse, frequently changing slices of the live transaction feed, such as all Mumbai activity or all large transactions, delivered immediately and without spawning new topics, so Solace handled that selective, low-latency routing. At the same time compliance needed every transaction stored durably for seven years and replayable to rebuild the ledger, so a bridge captured the same stream into Kafka, which we treated as the authoritative system of record. Solace made sure the right desk got the right event now; Kafka made sure nothing was ever lost and the whole history could be replayed later. That complementary split is why the two platforms so often live side by side in a bank.
